title: Stay Back
dateline: The night of the fish-market raid.
mood: A bent drone under a lamp, an old soldier’s screwdriver, and the two words her father always said.

hero.alt: Vexana, her long black hair loose over her Academy uniform, glances out at the viewer with a small, quiet smile.
hero.credit: Official Guinevere and Vexana comic, page 31

segs.t: Vexana put the phone face down beside the lamp. “Good,” she had told her, the way she did every night.
A crosswind,
she thought.
There was no wind on that roof.
The drone lay on her desk where she had set it down. One cat ear was bent flat. The bracket under it was twisted.

Her room was nearly bare. A tin of oil and a jar of spare screws stood beside two tactics books, stacked square. On the floor sat an old soldier’s toolbox, older than she was, its paint worn off at the handle. Guinevere had never been inside. Vexana always went to her.
She opened the drone’s shell with a thumbnail. From the toolbox she took a small screwdriver, its grip worn smooth where a thumb went, and loosened the bracket’s screw.
She set two fingers on the bracket, the way she had been taught. Her hand was shaking again. She waited. It went on shaking.
The screwdriver had been her father’s.
The Shield’s houses by the city wall.
Her mother had died of an illness before Vexana could remember her. So it had always been the two of them.

Her father was a soldier of the Shield of Dawnbreak, the defense force that fought the Enders. He kept the big guns on the city wall working. They lived in a row of Shield houses in the wall’s shadow.
He came home at dusk and set his boots by the door, toes to the wall. His uniform went over the chair, folded, corners square. He made tea and let it stew until it was black.
She tasted it once and spat it back into the cup. “It tastes like boots.”
“Soldier’s tea,” he said. “That’s how you know it’s working.”
On rest days he took her up into his gun pit. He hummed while he worked, always the same old march, and he always stopped in the same place.
“Why don’t you ever finish it?” she asked.
“It’s a long march,” he said. “I’ll finish it when the war does.”
When he held out his hand without looking, she put the right tool in it. He never had to say which.
One afternoon he showed her a bent bracket under a gun’s sight.
“A bent bracket makes a gun miss,” he said.

He set two fingers on it and pressed, slowly, until it was straight. He gave her a bent one from his spares. Her fingers were not strong enough, so she used both hands. It took her the rest of the afternoon.
He fitted it to the gun and sighted along it. “That one won’t miss.”
On her birthdays he took her up the wall stair, past the sleeping guns. The stair was steep. The first time, halfway up, her legs gave out, and he carried her the rest.
At the top there was only the dark ground beyond the wall, and stars over it. He pointed up and told her to look.
They gave the stars names. He named the bright ones after guns. She named hers after the kettle and the cat two doors down.
“That one’s yours,” he said. He pointed low, over the dark ground.
It was small. “Why that one?”
“It comes out first. Before it’s even dark.”
The wall houses had drills. When the drill bell rang, her father said two words. “Stay back.”
He went up to his gun, and she ran to the shelter at the end of the row. She sat on the bench by the door and kept still. She liked being the stillest one there.
When the all-clear sounded, he came and found her. “Good,” he said.
It was a game. Nothing bad ever happened in a drill.
One evening the bell rang while the tea was stewing. The guns on the wall began to fire, all of them at once. She had never heard that before.
This time he carried her to the shelter himself and knelt in the doorway.
“Stay back,” he said. Then he ran.
The shelter was full of strangers from the streets along the wall. The walls shook. Dust came down from the ceiling at every boom. A woman cried into her hands.
The all-clear did not sound. Her father did not come.
In a drill he always came before she got tired of sitting still. Now her legs had gone to sleep under her. At every boom she looked at the door.
An Ender was only a word in drills. She had never seen one.
If I’m with him, it’s all right,
she thought.
The door opened for a man carrying a child. She slipped out under his arm.
The street was full of smoke. She ran toward the wall stair. She knew the way.
Something had come over the wall. It stepped out of a side lane, a few steps from her, tall and gray. Smoke ran off its shoulders. A torn line of washing hung from one of its claws.
It did not look at her the way a person looks. It only stopped.
The claw came up.
Her feet would not move.
At the top of the stair, the gun she knew went quiet. Boots came down the stair at a run.
Her father was there, between her and it, his boots set wide on the stones. All she could see was his back in his Shield coat. One hand was out at his side, flat and still, the way it held a bracket.
“Stay back,” he said.
I will,
she thought.
I’ll go back. I’m sorry.
Her feet still would not move.
Arms caught her from behind. A soldier threw her over his shoulder and ran.
Over his shoulder she watched her father’s back. He stayed.
The smoke closed over him.
She shouted for him once. Her hands closed into fists. The soldier only ran faster.
Behind them the wall guns went on firing. The one she knew stayed quiet.
The Shield’s home for soldiers’ children.
The home stood behind the Shield’s barracks and ran on bells. Vexana came to it with one bag. Most of the children there had lost someone to the Enders.
On her second day a soldier from the wall brought her father’s toolbox. He set it by her cot.
“That Ender never got past him,” he said. “Not while he stood.”
She kept the toolbox under her cot. It smelled of gun oil.
At her first drill there, she sat in the shelter and kept still until the all-clear. Nobody came to find her. Nobody said “Good.”
That night she lay awake. Under the blanket she hummed his march. She stopped where he always stopped. Nobody knew the rest.
I didn’t stay back,
she thought.
He came back for me.
I only wanted to be with him. It should have been me.
After that she kept every rule. Nobody at the home ever had to tell her anything twice.
Each night she wiped the small screwdriver clean and put it back in its place. From the home’s yard she could not see past the barracks roofs. She never found her star there.
One morning a girl with two braids sat down beside her at breakfast and held out a blue ribbon. “You can have this one. Then we match.”
“No,” said Vexana.
The girl’s face fell. She took her bowl to another table.
People who stand near you die for you,
thought Vexana.
So nobody stands near me.
At dawn, before the bells, she trained alone in the yard with a wooden drill pole. Strike, turn, strike. The other children slept.
I owe him,
she thought.
I’ll pay it back in Enders.

Years went by like that. One dawn a young woman stood at the yard’s railings, watching. She wore a white officer’s coat, and a long rifle hung on her back. A dark visor covered one eye. She held a sheet of paper with the home’s stamp on it.
Vexana finished the drill before she looked up.
“Vexana,” said the woman. She read from the sheet. “Father, Shield of Dawnbreak. Killed in action.”
Vexana waited for the next part. People always said they were sorry.
The woman did not. “I’m Lesley. The Academy tests its first intake this year. Come.”
She folded the sheet and walked away without waiting for an answer.
At the Academy I could break more Enders,
thought Vexana. She picked up the pole again.
The morning of the entrance assessment.
Vexana walked across the city alone. The toolbox rode in a cloth bag on her shoulder. It was heavy. She had never thought of leaving it behind.
She was at the Academy gate when a long car stopped beside it, and she stood aside. A woman in a gray coat sat at the wheel.
A pink-haired girl climbed out of the back. Two red bows were tied in her hair, and she touched them both.
“Wait here,” said the girl.
“Yes, miss,” said the woman in the gray coat.
The girl walked in at the gate with her chin up, as if the place were already hers.
Like a lamp,
thought Vexana.
Someone that bright has never been in the dark.
She shifted the bag on her shoulder and walked past the pink-haired girl, eyes front, without a word.
